title: Miguel Pro (23 November)
hookLine: a Mexican Jesuit shot with his arms stretched out, saying long live Christ the King

lines: A YARD, A WALL, A LINE OF RIFLES.
cards: A yard in Mexico City. A wall. A line of men with rifles.
A priest in a plain suit is walked out to stand in front of them. According to the accounts handed down, he asks for one thing: a moment to pray. He kneels.
He prays. Then he gets up, and instead of folding his hands or bracing himself, he stretches his arms out wide, the shape of a cross, and says a few words in Spanish. Those words are today's line.

teach.h: A PRIEST IN HIDING, IN DISGUISE.
teach.b: Miguel Pro was a Jesuit priest at a time when the Mexican government had turned hard against the Church. Public worship stopped. Priests who stayed did their work in secret.
Pro stayed. The stories told about him are full of disguises: a mechanic in overalls, a beggar, a well-dressed young man strolling past the police.
He said Mass in private houses, heard confessions, and carried communion to people who couldn't get to a church. The stories are full of jokes too; he seems to have been funny, even in hiding.
Then came a failed attack on a former president, and Pro and his brothers were arrested.
The accounts say he had no part in it, and that he was shot without a trial.

teach.h: ARMS OUT: A PRAYER MADE WITH THE BODY.
teach.b: His last moment was a prayer made with the body. He knelt first. Then he stood with his arms out, the shape of the cross.
And the accounts say he forgave the men in front of him, which echoes what Jesus says from the cross in Luke's gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do."
The accounts give his last words as the cry of persecuted Catholics in Mexico in those years: viva Cristo Rey. Long live Christ the King. It isn't a curse on anyone.
It's a statement about who rules.
The soldiers held the rifles; he named a different king.
The Church declared him blessed, and in some places his day is kept on 23 November, close to the feast of Christ the King.

how: Blessed Miguel Agustín Pro is remembered on 23 November in some local calendars, including in Mexico and the United States, and Catholics there often pray for those who suffer for their faith.

games.q: you're Miguel Pro, a priest in a city where public worship has stopped. people still ask for the sacraments. what do you do?
o: leave the country until it's safe
stay, and reach them in disguise
write letters and wait it out
games.why: he stayed, in overalls and borrowed suits, saying Mass in private houses and bringing communion to people's doors.

practice: Sit up straight and slowly stretch your arms out to the sides, palms open, as wide as feels easy, and notice for a few breaths how open, and how unprotected, the body feels.
When your arms tire, rest your hands on your knees, palms up. If you pray, say the three words, viva Cristo Rey, quietly, once; if you don't, just stay with the open hands.

wordCard.voice: Miguel Pro. The Jesuit who served in disguise while churches were closed, and who died with his arms out, naming Christ as King.

orig.note: Spanish: long live Christ the King, the cry of persecuted Mexican Catholics and Miguel Pro's last words.

carryVoice: Your line: viva cristo rey. Even at the wall, his arms were open. See you tomorrow.
